client: I've been having a really hard time since my grandfather passed away last month. There's this constant heaviness in my chest, and some days I can barely get through work without feeling like I'm about to fall apart. I don't know if talking about it is actually going to change anything, but I figured I had to try something because I can't keep going on like this.
therapist: It takes real courage to reach out when you're carrying something this heavy, and I'm truly glad you decided to try. Grief can feel like this relentless weight that makes even ordinary moments feel almost impossible to get through, and what you're describing makes complete sense given the loss you've experienced. I'm curious — when that heaviness in your chest shows up during the day, what kinds of thoughts tend to be running through your mind in those moments?

client: Honestly, a lot of the time I'm thinking about things I never said to him, or times I was too busy to visit when I could have. There's this voice in my head that keeps telling me I should have been there more, like I wasted the time we had together. And then I feel guilty for even trying to function normally at work, like moving on with my day is somehow a betrayal of him.
therapist: That kind of quiet, persistent guilt is so painful to carry — it's like your mind has appointed itself a harsh judge, replaying moments and finding you guilty for simply being human and imperfect in your love for him. It's actually very common in grief for our minds to focus selectively on the "not enough" moments while overlooking all the ways we *were* present and caring. I'd gently like to ask — if your grandfather were here and could see the pain you're carrying right now, what do you think he would say to you about how you showed up in his life?

client: I want to say he would tell me I was a good grandchild and that he knew I loved him, but honestly it's hard to really believe that right now. Part of me thinks I'm just telling myself what I want to hear, like I'm letting myself off the hook too easily. It's easier to say what he might have said than to actually feel like it's true.
therapist: What strikes me is that you actually *do* know, somewhere inside you, what your grandfather thought — and yet your grief is making it feel unsafe to accept that comfort, as if believing it would somehow minimize the loss or let you off the hook. That inner critic isn't protecting him or honoring him; it's actually just keeping you in pain. What do you think it would mean for your relationship with his memory if you allowed yourself to genuinely receive that belief — that he knew he was loved?

client: I guess if I really let myself believe that, it might actually feel like... relief? But that's kind of what scares me, because I worry that if the guilt goes away, the grief will feel less intense, and then it's like he becomes less present somehow. I know that probably sounds strange, but the pain almost feels like the only connection I still have to him.
therapist: That doesn't sound strange at all — it actually makes profound sense, and it's one of the most tender things about grief, this fear that healing means losing them all over again. But I'd gently offer this: the love you had for him, the memories, the ways he shaped who you are — those don't live inside the pain, they live inside *you*, and they'll remain just as real when the guilt softens. What are some of the ways you can already feel his presence in your life that have nothing to do with the heaviness you're carrying?

client: There are little things, like I make coffee the same way he taught me, and sometimes I catch myself using phrases he used to say. When those moments happen, there's this brief flicker of something warm before the guilt rushes back in and kind of drowns it out. I never really thought about those things as a connection to him before, I always just pushed past them because they made me sad.
therapist: Those moments — the coffee, the phrases — those *are* him, still woven into your everyday life in the most real and lasting way. It's beautiful and significant that you're noticing them, even if the grief has been rushing in to overshadow that warmth before you can fully rest in it. I wonder what it might feel like to pause in one of those moments this week, just for a breath or two, and let yourself receive that warmth before moving on — almost like a small, intentional hello to him?

client: That actually sounds kind of nice when you describe it that way, but I'm worried that in the moment I'll just feel the sadness and not be able to hold onto the warmth long enough for it to mean anything. Like, I don't have a lot of practice sitting with good feelings without them turning heavy on me pretty quickly. I'm willing to try, but I guess I'm not very confident it'll work the way you're describing.
therapist: It's really honest and self-aware of you to notice that — and the fact that you're willing to try even without confidence is itself a meaningful step. The goal isn't to hold onto the warmth perfectly or for a long time; even just *noticing* it for a single breath before the heaviness arrives is a success, and like any skill, it can grow with gentle practice over time. What do you think gets in the way most when you try to stay with something that feels good — is it more the thoughts that rush in, or something that happens in your body?

client: I think it's mostly the thoughts, honestly. It's like the moment something feels okay, my brain immediately goes to "you don't deserve to feel okay right now" or "you're forgetting about him," and then my chest tightens up and the warmth is just gone. It's almost like my mind is on guard against anything that feels like relief.
therapist: You've just identified something really important — your mind has essentially set up a guard post against relief, treating any moment of peace as a threat rather than something you've earned. In CBT we'd call those rushing thoughts "automatic thoughts," and the key insight is that they feel like truth but they're actually just habits of thinking your mind developed to cope with the loss. What would you say to a close friend who told you they felt guilty for having one brief, warm moment while grieving someone they deeply loved?

client: I know I would tell a friend that one warm moment doesn't mean they've forgotten the person, and that it's okay to feel both grief and something good at the same time. But it's so much easier to extend that kind of compassion to someone else than to actually apply it to myself, and I don't really know why that gap exists. When it's me, the rules just feel different, like I'm a special case that doesn't get the same grace.
therapist: You've actually just uncovered something really central — you *know* the compassionate truth, you can say it clearly, and yet there's this deeply held belief that you're somehow exempt from receiving it yourself. That feeling of being a "special case" is so common, and it's worth gently questioning: what's the evidence that you actually deserve less grace than the friend you'd so readily comfort? It might be worth sitting with that question this week — not to force an answer, but just to notice what comes up when you ask yourself why the same rules don't apply to you.

client: When you put it that way, I genuinely can't think of a good reason why I deserve less grace, and that's a little unsettling to sit with because part of me has just accepted it as true without ever questioning it. I'll try to notice what comes up when I ask myself that question, but I'm a little worried it'll just turn into another thing I beat myself up about, like I'll ask the question and then feel guilty for not having a good enough answer. I don't want this to become another way my brain finds evidence against me.
therapist: That's such a wise and self-aware concern, and it tells me you're really starting to understand how your mind works — which is genuinely progress. So let's reframe the exercise slightly: rather than asking "why don't I deserve grace" as a question to *answer correctly*, treat it more like a gentle observation, almost like watching clouds pass — just noticing what thoughts arise without needing to grade yourself on them. The goal isn't to find the perfect answer; it's simply to get curious about a belief you've been carrying without ever choosing it. Does that feel like a version of the exercise you could approach a little more kindly?

client: Yeah, framing it as just watching rather than answering actually does feel less threatening, like I'm taking some of the pressure off myself to perform even in my own head. I think I can try that. I guess what I'm still sitting with is that this all feels like very new territory, because I've spent so long being hard on myself that I'm not even sure I'll recognize what self-compassion feels like when it shows up.
therapist: It's genuinely moving to hear you say that, because recognizing that self-compassion is unfamiliar territory *is* itself a form of self-awareness that takes courage to admit. And you might find that it doesn't announce itself dramatically — it may show up quietly, in small moments, like pausing over that cup of coffee without immediately pushing the warmth away. What do you think self-compassion might actually feel like in your body, even if it's just a tiny, unfamiliar flicker?
